unsure.label: Not sure
unsure.note: That's fine. Not knowing is common, and it's worth checking. We've counted it as something to look at, and the steps below show how.

profile.text: What kind of business is it?

Does your email address end in your own business name, like hello@yourbusiness.co.uk?

questions.text: When you log in to your business email, do you have to confirm it's you with your phone, a code or a passkey?
questions.help: This second step is called 2-step verification. A passkey lets you sign in with your face, fingerprint or phone PIN instead of a password.
questions.why: Your email is the key to everything else. With it, a criminal can reset your other passwords and send invoices that look like they came from you.
questions.example: A florist's email password is guessed. The criminal quietly reads invoices for a week, then emails a regular customer asking them to pay into a 'new' account.

questions.text: Is that second check also on for your business bank, social media, website, online storage and till or booking system?
questions.help: Most of these services have it in their security or account settings, often called '2-step verification', 'two-factor' or 'login approvals'.
questions.why: These accounts hold your money, your customers and your reputation. A stolen password alone shouldn't be enough to get in.
questions.example: A salon's Instagram is taken over and used to message clients a fake 'deposit' link.

questions.text: Does everyone use a different password for each work account, saved in a password manager or their phone's or browser's built-in one?
questions.help: A password manager remembers your passwords for you, so each one can be long and different.
questions.why: When one website is breached, criminals try the same email and password everywhere else. Different passwords stop one leak becoming many.
questions.example: A staff member reuses their gym password for the business email. The gym's site is breached, and the email is next.

questions.text: Where your email or other accounts offer passkeys, have you turned them on?
questions.help: A passkey signs you in with your face, fingerprint or phone PIN. There's nothing to type, so there's nothing for a scammer to trick you into sharing.
questions.why: The NCSC now recommends passkeys first, because they can't be phished or reused like passwords.
questions.example: A fake login page asks for a password. With a passkey there is no password to hand over.

questions.text: When someone leaves, do you remove their access to email, banking and other accounts on their last day?
questions.help: This includes shared passwords they knew, and any accounts set up for contractors or temps.
questions.why: Old accounts are easy to forget and often have old passwords. They're a common way in.
questions.example: A former employee's email is never closed. Months later it's used to send a fake invoice to a long-standing client.

questions.text: Does each person have their own login, rather than several people sharing one?
questions.help: Shared logins are things like one 'office@' account or one till login everybody uses.
questions.why: With shared logins you can't remove one person's access without changing it for everyone, and you can't see who did what.
questions.example: The whole team knows the bookings password. When someone leaves on bad terms, nobody changes it.

questions.text: Do only the people who need it have access to the bank account, payroll and customer records?
questions.help: This is sometimes called tiered access: people get what their job needs, and no more.
questions.why: The fewer people who can move money or see customer details, the fewer accounts a criminal can use to do damage.
questions.example: A part-time assistant's account can approve payments it never needs to. When it's hacked, so is the bank.

questions.text: Do you check who has access to your important accounts every few months?
questions.help: Look at the list of users on your email, bank, website and cloud storage, and remove anyone who shouldn't be there.
questions.why: People change roles and suppliers come and go. A quick review catches the accounts nobody remembers.
questions.example: A web designer from three years ago still has admin access to the shop's website.

questions.text: Are updates set to install automatically on your work computers, phones and tablets?
questions.help: Updates fix weaknesses that criminals know about. 'Automatic updates' is usually in the device's settings.
questions.why: Most attacks use weaknesses that already have a fix. Keeping up to date closes the door. Cyber Essentials expects security updates within 14 days.
questions.example: A shop laptop hasn't been updated in a year. A known weakness lets ransomware lock every file.

questions.text: Are all your work devices new enough to still get updates from the maker?
questions.help: Older phones and laptops stop getting updates after a few years. Your device's settings usually say if it's up to date.
questions.why: A device that no longer gets updates can't be fixed when a new weakness is found. You don't need the latest model, just a supported one.
questions.example: The till computer runs an old version of Windows that stopped getting security fixes years ago.

questions.text: Does every phone, tablet and laptop used for work lock with a PIN, password, face or fingerprint?
questions.help: This includes staff's own phones if they read work email or messages on them.
questions.why: Phones and tablets leave the building and get lost. A screen lock keeps customer details and accounts private if that happens.
questions.example: A tablet used for bookings is left in a café, unlocked, with every client's phone number on it.

questions.text: On work laptops and computers, do people use a standard account day to day, rather than the administrator account?
questions.help: The administrator account can install anything and change any setting. A standard account can't.
questions.why: If something nasty gets in while you're using a standard account, it can do far less damage.
questions.example: A fake 'invoice' attachment installs itself because it was opened on the administrator account.

questions.text: Do you back up the things your business needs to keep trading, such as customer records, invoices, emails and your website?
questions.help: A backup is a spare copy, either online (like OneDrive, Google Drive or iCloud) or on an external drive.
questions.why: If a device is lost or ransomware locks your files, a backup means you can carry on instead of starting from nothing.
questions.example: A builder's laptop is stolen from a van with two years of quotes and invoices on it, and no copy anywhere else.

questions.text: Is there a second copy kept apart, such as a drive you unplug after use, or an online backup protected with 2-step verification?
questions.help: Ransomware can reach a backup drive that stays plugged in. Unplugging it keeps the copy out of reach.
questions.why: Two copies kept in different ways mean one problem can't take out both.
questions.example: Ransomware locks the office computer and the backup drive that was left plugged into it.

questions.text: Have you tried restoring something from your backup to check it works?
questions.help: Pick one file or folder and get it back from the backup. It takes a few minutes.
questions.why: Many people find out their backup was incomplete only when they need it.
questions.example: A clinic's backup had been failing quietly for months. Nobody had checked.

questions.text: Do staff know how to report a suspicious email, and would they feel able to say so even if they'd already clicked the link?
questions.help: Reporting can be as simple as 'forward it to me and don't click anything'.
questions.why: The NCSC warns that blaming staff makes them hide mistakes. The sooner you hear about a click, the less damage it does.
questions.example: A new starter clicks a fake delivery link, feels embarrassed and says nothing for a week.

questions.text: Do you forward scam emails to the NCSC's free reporting service at report@phishing.gov.uk?
questions.help: It takes a minute. The NCSC checks the email and can take down the scam website.
questions.why: Reporting gets scam sites removed and protects other businesses too.
questions.example: A fake 'HMRC refund' email is forwarded, and the site behind it is taken down.

questions.text: Has your email or website provider set up the anti-spoofing records for your email address (called SPF, DKIM and DMARC)?
questions.help: These settings tell other email services which senders are really you, so scammers find it harder to fake your address.
questions.why: Without them, a criminal can send email that appears to come from your exact address to your customers and suppliers.
questions.example: Customers receive an email 'from' a café's own address asking them to update payment details.

questions.text: Have you checked what your website and social media reveal, such as staff names, roles and who your suppliers are?
questions.help: Criminals use these details to make scam emails sound like they come from someone you know.
questions.why: The less a scammer can learn about who pays whom, the harder it is to write a convincing fake.
questions.example: A 'Meet the team' page names the finance assistant. A week later she gets an email 'from the director' asking for an urgent payment.

questions.text: If a supplier asks to change their bank details, do you phone them on a number you already have, not one in the message, before paying?
questions.help: Use the number from an old invoice, your contacts or their official website. Never the one in the email or letter asking for the change.
questions.why: This one check stops most invoice fraud. It's rare for businesses to change bank accounts, so treat every request with care.
questions.example: A 'supplier' emails a new account number with their usual invoice. It's a lookalike email address, and the money is gone the same day.

questions.text: Do payments over a set amount need a second person to approve them?
questions.help: For example: one person sets up the payment and another checks and approves it.
questions.why: Government fraud guidance says no one person should both approve and pay. A second pair of eyes catches pressure and mistakes.
questions.example: An office manager, rushed by an 'urgent' email from the director, pays £8,400 with nobody else checking.

questions.text: Do new or changed bank details wait a few days before you pay them, so there's time to check?
questions.help: Some businesses wait 14 or 30 days before using new supplier bank details for the first time.
questions.why: Scammers rely on urgency. A built-in pause gives you time to confirm the change is real.
questions.example: A fake bank change arrives the day before a big payment run. The pause gives time for the real supplier to say 'that wasn't us'.

questions.text: Have you told staff that you, and anyone senior, will never ask for an urgent payment by email, text or phone call?
questions.help: A simple rule everyone knows makes a fake 'boss' request easy to spot.
questions.why: CEO fraud works by using authority and urgency. A known rule takes away both.
questions.example: 'I'm in a meeting, just pay this now and I'll explain later.' Staff who know the rule stop and check.

questions.text: Do your own invoices tell customers that your bank details won't change by email, and how to check if they're ever unsure?
questions.help: One line on your invoices, like 'Our bank details will never change by email. If in doubt, call us on our usual number.'
questions.why: Criminals also pretend to be you to your customers. Telling them what to expect gives them a chance to spot it.
questions.example: A customer receives a 'new bank details' email from a lookalike of your address, remembers the note on your invoices and calls you.

questions.text: Do you know what customer and staff information you hold, and where it's kept, such as email, spreadsheets, booking systems or paper?
questions.help: Personal information is anything that identifies someone: names, phone numbers, addresses, health notes, bank details.
questions.why: You can only protect what you know you have. It's also the first thing you'll need if information is ever lost.
questions.example: A salon keeps client allergy notes in a booking app, a spreadsheet and a paper diary, and only remembers two of them.

questions.text: Do you only collect the information you actually need?
questions.help: For example, a booking form that asks for a date of birth when you don't need it.
questions.why: UK GDPR says personal data should be limited to what you need. Less information held means less to lose.
questions.example: An online shop asks every customer for their date of birth and never uses it, until it's leaked.

questions.text: Do you delete customer information when you no longer need it, on a regular timetable?
questions.help: This is called a retention period: how long you keep each kind of record before deleting it.
questions.why: UK GDPR says not to keep personal data longer than you need it, and old records are a risk with no benefit.
questions.example: A breach exposes ten years of old customer records that nobody needed any more.

questions.text: If personal information was lost or stolen, would you know that you may need to tell the ICO within 72 hours, and how?
questions.help: The ICO is the UK's data protection regulator. Not every breach needs reporting, and the ICO has a tool to help you decide.
questions.why: If a breach is likely to put people at risk, the law expects you to report it, where feasible within 72 hours. Knowing in advance saves panic.
questions.example: A laptop with client records is stolen on Friday. On Monday the owner realises the 72 hours are nearly up.

questions.text: Do you have a list of the online services you rely on, such as your website, domain, payment provider, booking or till system and cloud storage?
questions.help: Just a simple list: the service, who has the login, and how to contact them.
questions.why: These accounts keep you trading. Knowing what they are is the first step to protecting them and recovering fast.
questions.example: The website goes down, and nobody knows which company hosts it or who has the login.

questions.text: When you choose an IT provider or an important supplier, do you ask about their security, for example whether they hold Cyber Essentials?
questions.help: Cyber Essentials is a government-backed scheme that shows an organisation has the basic protections in place.
questions.why: A supplier with weak security can become the way in to your business, or the source of a fake invoice.
questions.example: A supplier's email is hacked and used to send their customers invoices with new bank details.

questions.text: Is there a short written note of what to do in the first hour if you're hacked or scammed, with the numbers to call?
questions.help: One page is enough: who to call, what to switch off, and where to report it.
questions.why: In a crisis people freeze. A note on the wall means the right calls happen in the right order.
questions.example: A payment goes to a scammer at 4pm. Because the bank's fraud line is on the note, they call within minutes.

questions.text: Do you know where to report fraud or a cyber attack: your bank straight away, then Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040?
questions.help: Report Fraud replaced Action Fraud in December 2025. It's the police service for reporting fraud and cyber crime.
questions.why: Calling your bank fast gives the best chance of stopping a payment. Reporting helps the police and gets you support.
questions.example: A business realises it paid a fake invoice. Calling the bank within the hour, the payment is frozen before it leaves.

questions.text: Is one person named to take charge if something goes wrong, with a backup if they're away?
questions.help: It doesn't need to be an IT person. It just needs to be someone who will make the calls.
questions.why: When everyone assumes someone else is dealing with it, nobody is.
questions.example: The owner is on holiday when the email is hacked. Nobody knows who should decide what to do.

questions.text: Do you know which AI tools your team uses for work, including free personal accounts?
questions.help: AI tools include chatbots like ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini, and AI features inside apps you already use.
questions.why: You can't set sensible rules for tools you don't know about. Staff often use free AI tools on their own.
questions.example: A receptionist uses a free AI app on her phone to tidy up replies to clients, pasting in their messages.

questions.text: Have you chosen which AI tools are approved for work, and checked how each one uses what you type into it?
questions.help: Some AI services may keep or use what you type. Their settings or terms explain how.
questions.why: Picking approved tools, and setting them up properly, means work information goes to places you've checked.
questions.example: Two staff use five different AI apps between them. Nobody has read how any of them handle what's typed in.

questions.text: Have you told everyone never to paste customer details, staff records, passwords or bank details into AI tools?
questions.help: This includes copying in whole emails or documents that contain these details.
questions.why: Once typed into an AI tool, the information has left your business. AI tools can also be tricked into revealing what they've been given.
questions.example: A staff member pastes a customer's complaint, with their address and order history, into a free AI tool to draft a reply.

questions.text: When staff ask an AI tool for help with a real case, do they remove names and other identifying details first?
questions.help: For example, writing 'a customer' instead of a name, and leaving out addresses and order numbers.
questions.why: You usually get just as good an answer without the personal details. UK GDPR expects you to use only what you need.
questions.example: 'Help me reply to Sarah Jones at 12 Mill Lane about her refund' becomes 'Help me reply to a customer about a late refund'.

questions.text: Does a person check anything written by AI, such as emails, quotes or social posts, before customers see it?
questions.help: A quick read for facts, prices, promises and tone is enough.
questions.why: AI can state wrong things confidently. A wrong price, promise or fact sent to a customer is still your business's word.
questions.example: An AI-drafted reply promises a full refund the shop's policy doesn't offer, and the customer holds them to it.

questions.text: Does your chatbot hand over to a person for refunds, complaints and anything it isn't sure about?
questions.help: A handover can be as simple as 'I'll pass this to the team, who'll reply by email'.
questions.why: Chatbots can give confident wrong answers, and can be tricked by cleverly worded messages. Some topics need a person.
questions.example: A customer talks a chatbot into 'confirming' a discount that doesn't exist.

questions.text: Do you have a short written policy on using AI at work?
questions.help: One page covering which tools are approved, what never goes into them, and when a person must check the output.
questions.why: A clear policy turns good intentions into a habit, and gives new staff the rules from day one.
questions.example: A new starter assumes it's fine to use their personal AI account for client work, because nobody said otherwise.

questions.text: Have staff been shown real examples of what's fine to put into AI tools and what isn't?
questions.help: A 3-minute example session works better than a long policy nobody reads.
questions.why: People follow examples more easily than rules. Seeing what 'too much detail' looks like makes it stick.
questions.example: After a short session, staff start asking 'is this OK to paste?' before using AI.

questions.text: If 'the boss' called, sent a voice note or appeared on video asking for an urgent payment, would staff hang up and call back on a number they already have?
questions.help: AI can now copy someone's voice or face from a few online clips.
questions.why: Government fraud guidance warns that criminals impersonate senior people, sometimes with deepfake audio or video, to push urgent payments.
questions.example: A voice that sounds exactly like the owner calls the shop asking for £3,000 to be sent 'before the bank closes'.

questions.text: Do staff know that AI now writes scam emails with perfect spelling, so a well-written message isn't proof it's genuine?
questions.help: The old advice to look for spelling mistakes isn't enough any more.
questions.why: The NCSC says AI helps criminals write convincing phishing without the mistakes that used to give it away.
questions.example: A flawless, friendly email 'from the accountant' asks for staff payroll details.
